# Memory, Handles, Instrumentation, and Reliability

> **Draft chapter map.** Make resource identity, lifetime, memory budgets, and observability explicit engine services.

## Identity Before Address

- Explain why game code should name resources with stable handles rather than raw pointers or platform allocations.
- Relate identity to loading, replacement, serialization, and safe asynchronous work.

### Generational Handles and Resource Pools

- Introduce generational indices and slot-map-style arenas as a practical safe-handle pattern.
- Contrast stable identity with physical storage location.

#### Handle Failure Modes

- Cover stale handles, use-after-free prevention, and diagnostic-friendly invalidation.
- Establish what a handle can promise and what it deliberately cannot promise.

## Budgets Turn Failure into Policy

- Explain why CPU memory, GPU memory, upload bandwidth, and frame time need named limits.
- Frame budgets as arbitration rules among competing services rather than late-stage optimization.

### Resource Lifetime and Residency

- Distinguish logical asset lifetime from CPU and GPU residency.
- Connect eviction, streaming demand, and fallback behavior to explicit ownership.

#### Memory for Rust Engines

- Discuss how Rust’s safety model changes lifetime errors without eliminating capacity planning.
- Defer allocator and platform-specific details to implementation material.

## Instrumentation Is Part of the Architecture

- Establish profiling, tracing, and counters as data flows that must cross domains cleanly.
- Explain why a modern engine needs evidence before it can make budget decisions.

### Frame and Resource Telemetry

- Outline CPU timings, GPU timings, allocation pressure, queue depth, and streaming state.
- Distinguish current measurements from delayed or advisory feedback.

#### Designing for Diagnosis

- Show how stable names, scopes, and correlation IDs make cross-thread work understandable.
- Connect observability to AI-assisted development and reproducible performance work.

## Reliability Is an Engine Capability

- Establish tests, deterministic scenarios, and reproducible builds as architecture work rather than a final verification phase.
- Explain why cross-domain contracts need executable checks as well as prose and type signatures.

### Tests at Architectural Boundaries

- Cover unit, integration, property, and regression tests, with each form aimed at a different class of engine failure.
- Use fixed seeds, controlled clocks, and recorded inputs to make simulation and streaming failures repeatable.

#### Configuration, Features, and Delivery

- Treat configuration as validated data with clear ownership, defaults, and versioning rules.
- Cover feature policy, continuous integration, packaging, and cross-platform release checks as the path from a working engine to a dependable deliverable.
